title: Fluoride Supplement Fills Reached 14.5% of Young Children Without Fluoridated Water
html:
Only 14.5% of Massachusetts children ages 1–4 living without community water fluoridation had a filled prescription for an oral fluoride supplement, according to a research letter published Nov. 19 in JAMA Network Open.

Researchers analyzed 2022 enrollment and pharmacy claims from the Massachusetts all-payer claims database for 151,194 children enrolled in Medicaid or private insurance. They linked each child’s zip code to town-level fluoridation status. Among children with fluoridated water, who are least likely to need supplements, 0.8% had a fill. Across the full sample, the rate was 6.3%.

After adjustment for age, sex, insurance, and zip code characteristics, the probability of a fill was 14.2% for children without fluoridated water and 0.8% for those with it.

Fills were more common among Medicaid-enrolled children than privately insured children, at 7.3% vs. 4.8%. That difference was significant among children without fluoridated water. Among children with fluoridated water, fill rates did not differ significantly by insurance.

The American Academy of Pediatrics and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommend that primary care medical clinicians prescribe oral fluoride supplements for children 6 months through 4 years old in fluoride-deficient communities. The authors pointed to several possible barriers on the clinician side: limited screening for fluoridation status and limited knowledge of fluoride’s benefits. On the caregiver side, they cited difficulty filling prescriptions and fluoride hesitancy.

The authors framed the findings against recent pressure on fluoride access. They noted that Utah and Florida have banned community water fluoridation and that the CDC and EPA are investigating risks associated with it. They also noted that the FDA in 2025 signaled a possible ban on ingestible fluoride prescription products for children younger than 3, then issued a warning instead.

Ashley M. Kranz of RAND, Kimberley H. Geissler of UMass Chan Medical School–Baystate, and Lisa Simon of Harvard School of Dental Medicine conducted the study with funding from the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research.

The analysis covered a single state and may have misclassified fluoridation status at the zip code level. Supplements purchased without insurance, which cost less than $20 out of pocket, were not captured, so actual use may be underestimated.

Sources:
JAMA Network Open, “Oral Fluoride and Community Water Fluoridation Access Among Children,” published online Nov. 19, 2026: jamanetwork.com/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2856790
